title: MHT-CET 2025 (PCM) — Full Paper
description: Complete 150-question MHT-CET 2025 PCM paper: Physics, Chemistry (Section A) and Mathematics (Section B), with explanations.
instructions: This question booklet contains 150 Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs). Section-A: Physics & Chemistry - 50 Questions each; Section-B: Mathematics - 50 Questions.
Choice and sequence for attempting questions will be as per the convenience of the candidate.
Determine the one correct answer out of the four available options given for each question.
Each question with correct response shall be awarded one (1) mark. There shall be no negative marking.

questions.text: What is the effect of humidity on sound waves when humidity increases?

options.text: Speed of sound waves is more
Speed of sound waves is less
Speed of sound waves remains same
Speed of sound waves becomes zero

questions.explanation:
Speed of sound in a gas: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma RT}{M}}$.
Water vapour ($M = 18$) is lighter than dry air ($M \approx 29$). More humidity → lower average molar mass $M$ of the air → **higher** speed of sound.

questions.text: If $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are coefficient of linear, area and volume expansion respectively, then
questions.explanation:
For a cube of side $L$: $V + \Delta V = (L + \alpha L \Delta T)^3 \approx L^3(1 + 3\alpha\Delta T)$ (dropping $\alpha^2$, $\alpha^3$ terms).
Comparing with $V(1 + \gamma \Delta T)$ gives $\gamma = 3\alpha$. (Similarly $\beta = 2\alpha$, so option (c) is the trap.)

questions.text: A liquid is filled upto a height of 20 cm in a cylindrical vessel. The speed of liquid coming out of a small hole at the bottom of the vessel is ($g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$)
questions.explanation:
Torricelli's law: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 0.2} = \sqrt{4} = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Remember to convert 20 cm to 0.2 m.

questions.text: For a perfect gas, two pressures $P_1$ and $P_2$ are shown in figure. The graph shows:

options.text: Insufficient data to draw any conclusion

questions.explanation:
From $PV = nRT$: $V = \left(\dfrac{nR}{P}\right)T$, so the slope of a $V$–$T$ line is $\dfrac{nR}{P}$.
The $P_2$ line is steeper, so $\dfrac{nR}{P_2} > \dfrac{nR}{P_1}$ ⇒ $P_2 < P_1$, i.e. $P_1 > P_2$.

questions.text: A body of mass 2 kg moving with a speed of 4 m/s makes an elastic collision with another body at rest and continues to move in the original direction but with one fourth of its initial speed. The speed of the two body centre of mass is
questions.explanation:
After collision $v_1 = 4/4 = 1$ m/s. Elastic ($e = 1$): $v_2 - v_1 = u_1 - u_2 = 4$ ⇒ $v_2 = 5$ m/s.
Momentum: $2 \times 4 = 2 \times 1 + m_2 \times 5$ ⇒ $m_2 = \dfrac{6}{5}$ kg.
$v_{cm} = \dfrac{2 \times 4}{2 + 6/5} = \dfrac{8}{3.2} = 2.5$ m/s.
Shortcut: $v_{cm}$ doesn't change in a collision, so you can compute it with the *before* values.

questions.text: According to law of equipartition of energy the molar specific heat of a diatomic gas at constant volume where the molecule has one additional vibrational mode is :-
questions.explanation:
$C_V = \dfrac{f}{2}R$. A diatomic molecule has 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5 degrees of freedom.
One vibrational mode adds 2 (kinetic + potential) ⇒ $f = 7$, so $C_V = \dfrac{7}{2}R$.
Trap: counting the vibrational mode as only 1 gives $3R$, which isn't offered.

questions.text: As shown in the figure, a metallic rod of linear density $0.45\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$ is lying horizontally on a smooth incline plane which makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the horizontal. The minimum current flowing in the rod required to keep it stationary, when $0.15$ T magnetic field is acting on it in the vertical upward direction, will be : {Use $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$}
questions.explanation:
The magnetic force $F = ILB$ is horizontal (B is vertical). Balance along the incline:
$mg \sin 45^\circ = ILB \cos 45^\circ$ ⇒ $I = \dfrac{(m/L)\,g}{B}\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{0.45 \times 10}{0.15} = 30$ A.

questions.text: A sphere of radius $R$ carries charge density $\rho$ proportional to the square of the distance ($r$) from the centre such that $\rho = Cr^2$, where $C$ is a positive constant. At a distance $R/2$ from the centre, the magnitude of the electric field is
questions.explanation:
Gauss's law with a sphere of radius $r = R/2$:
$E \cdot 4\pi r^2 = \dfrac{1}{\epsilon_0}\displaystyle\int_0^{r} C r'^2 \cdot 4\pi r'^2\,dr' = \dfrac{4\pi C r^5}{5\epsilon_0}$
⇒ $E = \dfrac{C r^3}{5\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{C (R/2)^3}{5\epsilon_0} = \dfrac{CR^3}{40\epsilon_0}$.
This isn't among (a)–(c), so the answer is "None of these". Trap: option (c) is the field at the surface $r = R$.

questions.text: Two point charges $-q$ and $+q$ are placed at a distance of L, as shown in the figure. The magnitude of electric field intensity at a distance $R$ ($R \gg L$) varies as:
questions.explanation:
$-q$ and $+q$ separated by $L$ form an electric dipole. Far away ($R \gg L$) a dipole's field falls off as $E \propto \dfrac{p}{R^3}$.
Trap: $1/R^2$ is for a single point charge.

questions.text: The work done in increasing the size of a soap film from $10\ \text{cm} \times 6\ \text{cm}$ to $10\ \text{cm} \times 11\ \text{cm}$ is $3 \times 10^{-4}$ J. The surface tension of the film is
questions.explanation:
A soap film has **two** surfaces: $W = S \times 2\Delta A$.
$\Delta A = (110 - 60)\ \text{cm}^2 = 50 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$
$S = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 50 \times 10^{-4}} = 3 \times 10^{-2}$ N/m.
Trap: forgetting the factor 2 gives option (b).

questions.text: A sample of gas expands from volume $V_1$ to $V_2$. The amount of work done by the gas is greatest when the expansion is
questions.explanation:
Work = area under the $P$–$V$ curve. Starting from the same state and going from $V_1$ to $V_2$:
- isobaric: pressure stays at its initial value → largest area,
- isothermal: pressure falls as $1/V$,
- adiabatic: pressure falls fastest ($PV^\gamma$ = const) → smallest area.
So $W_{\text{isobaric}} > W_{\text{isothermal}} > W_{\text{adiabatic}}$.
Note: the published answer key for this paper lists (a) isothermal, which is incorrect for an expansion between the same volumes.

questions.text: The figure below shows currents in a part of electric circuit. The current $i$ is
questions.explanation:
Kirchhoff's junction rule (current in = current out):
First junction: $2 + 2 = 4$ A flows on.
Second junction: 1 A leaves, so $4 - 1 = 3$ A continues.
Last junction: $3 = 1.3 + i$ ⇒ $i = 1.7$ A.

questions.text: Two discs of moment of inertia $I_1$ and $I_2$ and angular speeds $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are rotating along collinear axes passing through their centre of mass and perpendicular to their plane. If the two are made to rotate combindly along the same axis the rotational KE of system will be
questions.explanation:
No external torque ⇒ angular momentum is conserved: $I_1\omega_1 + I_2\omega_2 = (I_1 + I_2)\omega$ ⇒ $\omega = \dfrac{I_1\omega_1 + I_2\omega_2}{I_1 + I_2}$.
$KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(I_1 + I_2)\omega^2 = \dfrac{(I_1\omega_1 + I_2\omega_2)^2}{2(I_1 + I_2)}$.
Option (a) has the wrong dimensions (not energy) — a quick way to eliminate it.

questions.text: If a current is passed in a spring, it
questions.explanation: Neighbouring turns of the spring carry current in the **same** direction. Parallel currents in the same direction attract, so the turns pull together and the spring gets compressed.

questions.text: A long solenoid carrying a current produces a magnetic field $B$ along its axis. If the current is doubled and the number of turns per cm is halved, the new value of magnetic field will be equal to
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0 n I$. New field: $B' = \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right)(2I) = \mu_0 n I = B$.

questions.text: Hail stroms are observed to strike the surface of the frozen lake at $30^\circ$ with the vertical and rebound at $60^\circ$ with the vertical. Assume contact to be smooth, the coefficient of restitution is :
questions.explanation:
Smooth surface ⇒ the component **parallel** to the surface is unchanged: $u \sin 30^\circ = v \sin 60^\circ$ ⇒ $v = \dfrac{u}{\sqrt{3}}$.
$e = \dfrac{\text{normal speed after}}{\text{normal speed before}} = \dfrac{v\cos 60^\circ}{u\cos 30^\circ} = \dfrac{\frac{u}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac12}{u\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.text: Following figure shows two processes A and B for a gas. If $\Delta Q_A$ and $\Delta Q_B$ are the amount of heat absorbed by the system in two cases, and $\Delta U_A$ and $\Delta U_B$ are changes in internal energies, respectively, then:
questions.explanation:
Internal energy is a state function: both paths go from $i$ to $f$, so $\Delta U_A = \Delta U_B$.
Path A lies above B on the $P$–$V$ diagram, so the area under it is larger: $W_A > W_B$.
$\Delta Q = \Delta U + W$ ⇒ $\Delta Q_A > \Delta Q_B$.

questions.text: Two identical coils each of self-inductance L, are connected in series and are placed so close to each other that all the flux from one coil links with the other. The total self-inductance of the system is:
questions.explanation:
Perfect flux linkage ⇒ coupling coefficient $k = 1$, so $M = k\sqrt{L_1 L_2} = L$.
Series, fluxes aiding: $L_{eq} = L_1 + L_2 + 2M = L + L + 2L = 4L$.
Trap: ignoring mutual inductance gives $2L$.

questions.text: In a moving coil galvanometer, the deflection of the coil $\theta$ is related to the elecrical current $i$ by the relation
questions.explanation:
In equilibrium, deflecting torque = restoring torque: $NIAB = C\theta$ ⇒ $i = \dfrac{C}{NAB}\theta$, so $i \propto \theta$ (the radial field makes the scale linear).
$i \propto \tan\theta$ is the tangent galvanometer — a common mix-up.

questions.text: Metals getting magnetised by orientation of atomic magnetic moments in external magnetic field are called
questions.explanation:
Paramagnetic atoms have permanent magnetic moments that are randomly oriented; an external field partially **aligns** them, magnetising the material (weakly, in the field direction).
Diamagnetism comes from induced moments opposing the field (no permanent moments); ferromagnetism involves domains.

questions.text: A step up transformer operates on a 230 V line and supplies a current of 2 ampere. The ratio of primary and secondary winding is 1:25. The current in primary is
questions.explanation:
For an ideal transformer $\dfrac{I_p}{I_s} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = 25$.
Secondary current $I_s = 2$ A ⇒ $I_p = 25 \times 2 = 50$ A.
A step-up transformer raises voltage and lowers current, so the primary current must be larger than the secondary.

questions.text: The four arms of a Wheatstone bridge have resistances as shown in the figure. A galvanometer of $15\,\Omega$ resistance is connected across BD. Calculate the current through the galvanometer when a potential difference of 10 V is maintained across AC.
questions.explanation:
The bridge is unbalanced ($100/10 \neq 60/5$), so use nodal analysis with $V_A = 10$ V, $V_C = 0$.
Node B: $\dfrac{V_B - 10}{100} + \dfrac{V_B - V_D}{15} + \dfrac{V_B}{10} = 0$ ⇒ $53V_B - 20V_D = 30$
Node D: $\dfrac{V_D - 10}{60} + \dfrac{V_D - V_B}{15} + \dfrac{V_D}{5} = 0$ ⇒ $-4V_B + 17V_D = 10$
Solving: $V_B \approx 0.865$ V, $V_D \approx 0.792$ V.
$I_G = \dfrac{V_B - V_D}{15} = \dfrac{0.073}{15} \approx 4.87 \times 10^{-3}$ A $= 4.87$ mA.

questions.text: The net impedance of circuit (as shown in figure) will be
questions.explanation:
$X_L = 2\pi f L = 2\pi \times 50 \times \dfrac{50}{\pi} \times 10^{-3} = 5\ \Omega$
$X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times \frac{10^3}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}} = 10\ \Omega$
$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2} = \sqrt{10^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{125} = 5\sqrt{5}\ \Omega$.

questions.text: Two conducting circular loops of radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ are placed in the same plane with their centres coinciding. If $R_1 \gg R_2$, the mutual inductance $M$ between them will be directly proportional to
questions.explanation:
Pass current $i$ in the big loop. Its field at the centre is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 i}{2R_1}$, nearly uniform over the small loop since $R_1 \gg R_2$.
Flux through the small loop: $\phi = B \cdot \pi R_2^2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi R_2^2}{2R_1} i = Mi$
⇒ $M = \dfrac{\mu_0 \pi R_2^2}{2R_1} \propto \dfrac{R_2^2}{R_1}$.

questions.text: In a circuit, L, C and R are connected in series with an alternating voltage source of frequency f. The current leads the voltage by $45^\circ$. The value of C is
questions.explanation:
Current leads ⇒ the circuit is capacitive: $\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{X_C - X_L}{R} = 1$
⇒ $\dfrac{1}{\omega C} = R + \omega L$ ⇒ $C = \dfrac{1}{\omega(R + \omega L)} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi f(R + 2\pi f L)}$.

questions.text: If a thin prism of glass is dipped in water then minimum deviation of light produced by prism will be (as a fraction of the prism angle $A$) $\left({}_a\mu_g = \tfrac{3}{2},\ {}_a\mu_w = \tfrac{4}{3}\right)$
questions.explanation:
For a thin prism $\delta = (\mu - 1)A$, where $\mu$ is the refractive index of glass **relative to the surrounding medium**.
In water: $\,{}_w\mu_g = \dfrac{3/2}{4/3} = \dfrac{9}{8}$ ⇒ $\delta_m' = \left(\dfrac{9}{8} - 1\right)A = \dfrac{1}{8}A$.
(In air it would be $\tfrac{1}{2}A$, so the deviation drops to a quarter in water.)

questions.text: A liquid does not wet the solid surface if angle of contact is
questions.explanation:
Angle of contact $< 90^\circ$ ⇒ the liquid wets the surface (e.g. water on glass).
Angle of contact $> 90^\circ$ (obtuse) ⇒ it does **not** wet the surface (e.g. mercury on glass).

questions.text: In the double slit experiment, the monochromatic source is shifted to a position $S'$ at an angle $\phi$ above $SQ$. The position of central bright fringe will be
questions.explanation:
The central bright fringe is where the total path difference (source → slit → screen) is zero.
Moving the source up by angle $\phi$ makes the path via $S_2$ longer before the slits, so it must be shorter after them: the central fringe moves **down**, to the point at angle $\phi$ below the axis, on the line through $S'$ and the midpoint $Q$ of the slits. That point is $O''$.

questions.text: If the radius of a nucleus $\,{}^{256}X$ is 8 fermi, then the radius of $\,{}^{4}\text{He}$ nucleus will be

Four identical solid spheres each of mass 'm' and radius 'a' are placed with their centres on the four corners of a square of side 'b'. The moment of inertia of the system about one side of square where the axis of rotation is parallel to the plane of the square is :
questions.explanation:
Each sphere about its own diameter: $\tfrac{2}{5}ma^2$.
Two spheres lie **on** the axis: $2 \times \tfrac{2}{5}ma^2$.
Two spheres are at distance $b$ (parallel axis theorem): $2\left(\tfrac{2}{5}ma^2 + mb^2\right)$.
Total: $I = \tfrac{8}{5}ma^2 + 2mb^2$.

questions.text: Two sources of light emit X-rays of wavelength 1 nm and visible light of wavelength 500 nm, respectively. Both the sources emit light of the same power 200 W. The ratio of the number density of photons of X-rays to the number density of photons of the visible light of the given wavelengths is :
questions.explanation:
Photons per second $n = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{P\lambda}{hc}$, so at equal power $n \propto \lambda$.
$\dfrac{n_X}{n_{vis}} = \dfrac{1}{500}$. Higher-energy (X-ray) photons → fewer of them for the same power.

questions.text: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with air as medium is $6\ \mu$F. With the introduction of a dielectric medium, the capacitance becomes $30\ \mu$F. The permittivity of the medium is : ($\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$)
Sodium and copper have work functions 2.3 eV and 4.5 eV respectively. Then the ratio of the wavelengths is nearest to
questions.explanation:
Threshold wavelength $\lambda_0 = \dfrac{hc}{W_0}$, so $\lambda_0 \propto \dfrac{1}{W_0}$.
$\dfrac{\lambda_{Na}}{\lambda_{Cu}} = \dfrac{4.5}{2.3} \approx 2 : 1$.

questions.text: When the number of nucleons in nuclei increases, the binding energy per nucleon

options.text: first increases and then decreases with increase of mass number

questions.explanation: On the binding-energy curve, BE/nucleon rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks around $A \approx 56$ (iron, ~8.8 MeV), then slowly decreases for heavy nuclei. That's why both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei release energy.

questions.text: Three capacitors $2\ \mu$F, $3\ \mu$F and $6\ \mu$F are joined in series with each other. The equivalent capacitance is-
questions.explanation:
Series: $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{3 + 2 + 1}{6} = 1$ ⇒ $C = 1\ \mu$F.
Check: in series the result is always smaller than the smallest capacitor (2 μF). $11\ \mu$F is the parallel combination.

questions.text: The energy levels of an hydrogen atom are shown below. The transition corresponding to emission of shortest wavelength is
questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$: shortest wavelength ⇔ largest energy gap.
Transition D ends on $n = 1$ (from $n = 3$, $\Delta E = 12.09$ eV), far larger than the others, which end on $n = 2$ or $n = 3$. So D.

questions.text: A logic gate circuit has two inputs A and B and output Y. The voltage waveforms of A, B and Y are shown below. The logic gate circuit is
questions.explanation:
Read the waveforms interval by interval: Y is high whenever **at least one** input is high, and low only when both A and B are low.
A=0, B=0 → Y=0
A=0, B=1 → Y=1
A=1, B=0 → Y=1
A=1, B=1 → Y=1
That truth table is an OR gate.

questions.text: The ratio of frequencies of fundamental harmonic produced by an open pipe to that of closed pipe having the same length is
questions.explanation:
Open pipe: $f_o = \dfrac{v}{2l}$. Closed pipe: $f_c = \dfrac{v}{4l}$.
$\dfrac{f_o}{f_c} = \dfrac{4l}{2l} = 2 : 1$.

questions.text:
Consider the following statements and select the correct option.
(i) The ratio of $C_P / C_V$ for a diatomic gas is more than that of a monoatomic gas.
(ii) The ratio of $C_P / C_V$ is more for helium gas than for hydrogen
questions.explanation:
$\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}$: monoatomic ($f = 3$) $\gamma = 1.67$; diatomic ($f = 5$) $\gamma = 1.4$.
(i) is false: diatomic has the **smaller** $\gamma$.
(ii) is true: He (monoatomic, 1.67) > H₂ (diatomic, 1.4).

questions.text: In an unbiased p-n junction electrons diffuse from n-region to p-region because :

options.text: electrons travel across the junction due to potential difference
electron concentration in n-region is more compared to that in p-region

questions.explanation:
Diffusion is driven by a **concentration gradient**: electrons move from where they are plentiful (n-side) to where they are scarce (p-side).
The potential difference across the junction actually opposes this diffusion (it builds up the depletion region), so (b) is wrong.

questions.text: A particle is travelling 4 times as fast as an electron. Assuming the ratio of de-Broglie wavelength of a particle to that of electron is 2 : 1, the mass of the particle is
questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$ ⇒ $m = \dfrac{h}{\lambda v}$.
$\dfrac{m_p}{m_e} = \dfrac{\lambda_e v_e}{\lambda_p v_p} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{8}$.

questions.text: Consider a Young's double slit experiment as shown in figure. What should be the slit separation d in terms of wavelength $\lambda$ such that the first minima occurs directly in front of the slit ($S_1$)?
questions.explanation:
Screen distance $D = 2d$. Point P is directly in front of $S_1$.
$S_1P = 2d$; $S_2P = \sqrt{(2d)^2 + d^2} = \sqrt{5}\,d$.
First minimum: path difference $= \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ ⇒ $\sqrt{5}d - 2d = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$ ⇒ $d = \dfrac{\lambda}{2(\sqrt{5} - 2)}$.
Here $D$ is comparable to $d$, so the usual small-angle formula $y = \frac{D\lambda}{2d}$ does **not** apply.

questions.text: A simple pendulum performs SHM about $x = 0$ with an amplitude $a$ and time period $T$. What is the speed of the pendulum at $x = a/2$?
questions.explanation: $v = \omega\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}\sqrt{a^2 - \dfrac{a^2}{4}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}a}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\pi a}{T}$.

questions.text: An astronomical telescope has a magnifying power 10, the focal length of the eyepiece is 20 cm. The focal length of the objective is
questions.explanation:
Normal adjustment: $M = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}$ ⇒ $f_o = 10 \times 20 = 200$ cm.
A telescope needs a long-focus objective, so the tiny values in (a), (b), (d) can be ruled out immediately.

questions.text: Find the torque about the origin when a force of $3\hat{j}$ N acts on a particle whose position vector is $2\hat{k}$ m.
questions.explanation:
$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = 2\hat{k} \times 3\hat{j} = 6(\hat{k} \times \hat{j}) = 6(-\hat{i}) = -6\hat{i}$ Nm.
Remember the cyclic order $\hat{i} \to \hat{j} \to \hat{k}$: going backwards ($\hat{k} \times \hat{j}$) gives a minus sign.

questions.text: A planet of mass m moves around the sun of mass M in an elliptical orbit. The maximum and minimum distance of the planet from the sun are $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively. The time period of planet is proportional to
questions.explanation:
Kepler's third law: $T^2 \propto a^3$, where $a$ is the semi-major axis.
For an ellipse, $a = \dfrac{r_{max} + r_{min}}{2} = \dfrac{r_1 + r_2}{2}$ ⇒ $T \propto \left(\dfrac{r_1 + r_2}{2}\right)^{3/2}$.

questions.text: Consider a planet in some solar system which has a mass double the mass of earth and density equal to the average density of earth. If the weight of an object on earth is W, the weight of the same object on that planet will be :
questions.explanation:
Same density, double mass ⇒ double volume ⇒ $R_P = 2^{1/3}R_E$.
$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ ⇒ $\dfrac{g_P}{g_E} = \dfrac{2}{(2^{1/3})^2} = 2^{1 - 2/3} = 2^{1/3}$.
So weight on the planet $= 2^{1/3}W$. (Shortcut: at fixed density, $g \propto R$.)

questions.text: A bucket tied at the end of a 1.6 m long string is whirled in a vertical circle with constant speed. What should be the minimum speed so that the water from the bucket does not spill when the bucket is at the highest position?
questions.explanation: At the top, gravity alone must supply the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \ge mg$ ⇒ $v_{min} = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{10 \times 1.6} = 4$ m/s.

questions.text: The minimum velocity (in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$) with which a car driver must traverse a flat curve of radius 150 m and coefficient of friction 0.6 to avoid skidding is
questions.explanation:
On a flat curve friction provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} \le \mu mg$ ⇒ $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu r g} = \sqrt{0.6 \times 150 \times 10} = 30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
(The question says "minimum", but physically this is the **maximum** safe speed; the intended answer is 30.)

questions.text: Mean free path of a gas molecule is

options.text: inversely proportional to number of molecules per unit volume
inversely proportional to diameter of the molecule
directly proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature
directly proportional to the molecular mass

questions.explanation:
$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n}$, where $n$ = molecules per unit volume and $d$ = molecular diameter.
So $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{n}$ (a). It goes as $\dfrac{1}{d^2}$, not $\dfrac{1}{d}$, so (b) is wrong.

questions.text: Identify the species having one $\pi$-bond and maximum number of canonical forms from the following :
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$ has one C=O π-bond that can sit on any of the three oxygens → **3 equivalent canonical structures**.
$\mathrm{SO_2}$ has 2 resonance forms; $\mathrm{SO_3}$ has three π-bonds (S=O) in its usual Lewis structure; $\mathrm{O_2}$ has one π-bond but no resonance.

questions.text: The shortest wavelength of hydrogen atom in Lyman series is $\lambda$. The longest wavelength in Balmer series of $\mathrm{He^+}$ is
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$
H, Lyman shortest ($\infty \to 1$): $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R$.
$\mathrm{He^+}$ ($Z = 2$), Balmer longest ($3 \to 2$): $\dfrac{1}{\lambda'} = 4R\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = \dfrac{5R}{9}$
⇒ $\lambda' = \dfrac{9}{5R} = \dfrac{9\lambda}{5}$.

questions.text: Number of atoms in the following samples of substances is the largest in :
questions.explanation:
Count moles of **atoms**:
$\mathrm{H_2}$: $4/2 = 2$ mol molecules = **4 mol atoms**
$\mathrm{Cl_2}$: $71/71 = 1$ mol = 2 mol atoms
$\mathrm{I_2}$: $127/254 = 0.5$ mol = 1 mol atoms
Mg: $48/24 = 2$ mol atoms
Largest: 4.0 g of hydrogen.

questions.text: van der Waals equation for a gas is stated as, $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V - nb} - a\left(\dfrac{n}{V}\right)^2$. This equation reduces to the perfect gas equation, $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V}$ when,

options.text: temperature is sufficient high and pressure is low.
temperature is sufficient low and pressure is high.
both temperature and pressure are very high.
both temperature and pressure are very low.

questions.explanation:
Rewrite as $\left(P + \dfrac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$.
At **low pressure** the volume is large, so $nb \ll V$ and $\dfrac{an^2}{V^2}$ is negligible; at **high temperature** molecules move fast, so attractions ($a$) don't matter. Then $PV = nRT$.

questions.text: Copper crystallises in fcc with a unit length of 361 pm. What is the radius of copper atom?
questions.explanation:
In fcc, atoms touch along the face diagonal: $4r = \sqrt{2}a$ ⇒ $r = \dfrac{a}{2\sqrt{2}} = 0.3535a$.
$r = 0.3535 \times 361 \approx 128$ pm.

questions.text: For an ideal solution of two components A and B, which of the following is true?

options.text: A – B interaction is stronger than A – A and B – B interactions
A– A, B – B and A – B interactions are identical.

questions.explanation:
An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law exactly because A–B interactions are the same as A–A and B–B interactions. Consequences: $\Delta H_{mix} = 0$ and $\Delta V_{mix} = 0$.
(c) describes a solution with **negative** deviation, not an ideal one.

questions.text: Correct order of limiting molar conductivity for cations in water at 298 K is :
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{H^+}$ is exceptional (Grotthuss "proton hopping"): ≈ 350 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Higher charge → higher molar conductivity: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ (≈119) > $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ (≈106; smaller ion, more heavily hydrated, so slower).
Among +1 ions, the larger $\mathrm{K^+}$ is less hydrated and moves faster than $\mathrm{Na^+}$: 73.5 vs 50.1.
Order: $\mathrm{H^+ > Ca^{2+} > Mg^{2+} > K^+ > Na^+}$.

questions.text: The statement that is **not** true about ozone is :

options.text: in the stratosphere, CFCs release chlorine free radicals ($\dot{\mathrm{Cl}}$) which reacts with $\mathrm{O_3}$ to give chlorine dioxide radicals.
in the atmosphere, it is depleted by CFCs.
in the stratosphere, it forms a protective shield against UV radiation.
it is a toxic gas and its reaction with NO gives $\mathrm{NO_2}$.

questions.explanation:
$\dot{\mathrm{Cl}} + \mathrm{O_3} \to \mathrm{Cl\dot{O}} + \mathrm{O_2}$ — the product is the chlorine **monoxide** radical (ClO•), not chlorine dioxide. So (a) is the false statement.
(d) is true: $\mathrm{NO + O_3 \to NO_2 + O_2}$.

questions.text: The density of 'x' M solution ('x' molar) of NaOH is 1.12 g mL⁻¹, while in molality, the concentration of the solution is 3 m (3 molal). Then x is (Given : Molar mass of NaOH is 40 g/mol)
questions.explanation:
Take 1 L of solution: mass = 1120 g, NaOH = $40x$ g, water = $1120 - 40x$ g.
Molality $= \dfrac{x \times 1000}{1120 - 40x} = 3$ ⇒ $1000x = 3360 - 120x$ ⇒ $x = 3.0$.

questions.text: Identify the correct trend given below : (Atomic No. = Ti : 22, Cr : 24 and Mo : 42)
questions.explanation:
Two rules for crystal-field splitting $\Delta_o$:
1. Higher oxidation state of the metal → larger $\Delta_o$: $\mathrm{Ti^{3+}} > \mathrm{Ti^{2+}}$.
2. Going down a group (3d → 4d → 5d) $\Delta_o$ increases (more diffuse d-orbitals interact more with ligands): Mo (4d) > Cr (3d).
Both match (c).

questions.text: Halogenation of which one of the following will yield m-substituted product with respect to methyl group as a major product?
questions.explanation:
The incoming halogen goes where the **strongest activating group** directs it.
In o-cresol (c), –OH (+M) is a much stronger activator than –CH₃ (+I/hyperconjugation), so substitution goes ortho/para to –OH. The position para to –OH is **meta** to –CH₃.
In (a), (b), (d) the second group (–CHO, –NO₂) is deactivating, so –CH₃ controls and directs ortho/para to itself.

questions.text: An element crystallises in a face-centred cubic (fcc) unit cell with cell edge $a$. The distance between the centres of two nearest octahedral voids in the crystal lattice is :
questions.explanation:
In fcc, octahedral voids sit at the **body centre** and at the **12 edge centres**.
Body centre $(\tfrac{a}{2}, \tfrac{a}{2}, \tfrac{a}{2})$ to the edge centre $(\tfrac{a}{2}, 0, 0)$:
$x = \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{a}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ (the same as between two adjacent edge centres).
No two voids are closer, so the answer is $\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$.

questions.text: The correct order of stability of following carbocations is:
questions.explanation:
Priority: aromaticity > resonance > hyperconjugation.
C (tropylium ion) is **aromatic** (6π electrons, planar ring) → most stable.
A (triphenylmethyl) has three phenyl rings for resonance > B (diphenylmethyl) with two.
D (sec-butyl) has only hyperconjugation/+I → least stable.
So C > A > B > D.

questions.text: The correct order of bond orders of $\mathrm{C_2^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{N_2^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}$ is, respectively.
questions.explanation:
Bond order $= \dfrac{N_b - N_a}{2}$:
$\mathrm{C_2^{2-}}$ (14 e⁻, isoelectronic with N₂): 3
$\mathrm{N_2^{2-}}$ (16 e⁻, isoelectronic with O₂): 2
$\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}$ (18 e⁻, peroxide): 1
Increasing order: $\mathrm{O_2^{2-} < N_2^{2-} < C_2^{2-}}$.

questions.text: Oxidation number of potassium in $\mathrm{K_2O}$, $\mathrm{K_2O_2}$ and $\mathrm{KO_2}$, respectively, is:
questions.explanation: An alkali metal is **always +1** in its compounds. What changes is the oxygen: oxide $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ (−2), peroxide $\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}$ (−1 each), superoxide $\mathrm{O_2^{-}}$ (−½ each).

questions.text: Sodium metal on dissolution in liquid ammonia gives a deep blue solution due to the formation of:
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{Na + (x + y)NH_3 \to [Na(NH_3)_x]^+ + [e(NH_3)_y]^-}$
The **ammoniated (solvated) electrons** absorb red light, so the solution looks blue; they also make it conducting and paramagnetic.

questions.text: The emf of cell $\mathrm{Tl\,|\,Tl^+(0.001\,M)\,||\,Cu^{2+}(0.01\,M)\,|\,Cu}$ is 0.83 V at 298 K. It could be increased by :

options.text: increasing concentration of both $\mathrm{Tl^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ions
decreasing concentration of both $\mathrm{Tl^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ions

questions.explanation:
Cell reaction: $\mathrm{2Tl + Cu^{2+} \to 2Tl^+ + Cu}$
$E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.0591}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Tl^+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}$
$E$ increases when $[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]$ (reactant) increases or $[\mathrm{Tl^+}]$ (product) decreases. So (d).

questions.text: The reaction at cathode in the cells commonly used in clocks involves.
questions.explanation:
Clock cells are dry (Leclanché) cells. Cathode: $\mathrm{MnO_2 + NH_4^+ + e^- \to MnO(OH) + NH_3}$
Mn goes from +4 (in MnO₂) to +3 (in MnO(OH)) — a reduction, as always at the cathode.

questions.text: Which of the following complex is homoleptic?
questions.explanation: Homoleptic = only **one kind** of ligand around the metal. $\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}$ has only CN⁻. The others mix NH₃ and Cl⁻, so they are heteroleptic.

questions.text: The complex that can show optical activity is :
questions.explanation:
Optical activity needs a structure with **no plane of symmetry**.
$cis$-$\mathrm{[M(AA)_2X_2]}$ (two bidentate ligands + two cis monodentate ligands) is chiral — like cis-[Co(en)₂Cl₂]⁺ — so (d).
The trans isomers have a mirror plane; $\mathrm{[M A_2 B_4]}$ with only monodentate ligands (b, c) also always has one.

questions.text: A solution of $\mathrm{Ni(NO_3)_2}$ is electrolysed between platinum electrodes using 0.1 Faraday electricity. How many mole of Ni will be deposited at the cathode?
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{Ni^{2+} + 2e^- \to Ni}$: 2 F deposit 1 mol Ni.
0.1 F deposits $\dfrac{0.1}{2} = 0.05$ mol.

questions.text: In a first order decomposition reaction, the time taken for the decomposition of reactant to one fourth and one eighth of its initial concentration are $t_1$ and $t_2$ (s), respectively. The ratio $\dfrac{t_1}{t_2}$ will :
questions.explanation:
First order: $t = \dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]}$.
$t_1 = \dfrac{\ln 4}{k} = \dfrac{2\ln 2}{k}$ (2 half-lives), $t_2 = \dfrac{\ln 8}{k} = \dfrac{3\ln 2}{k}$ (3 half-lives).
$\dfrac{t_1}{t_2} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.text: The strongest reducing agent among the following is:
questions.explanation: Down group 15 the E–H bond gets longer and weaker, so thermal stability of the hydrides falls from $\mathrm{NH_3}$ to $\mathrm{BiH_3}$ and their **reducing character increases**. $\mathrm{BiH_3}$ is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.text: $t_{1/4}$ can be taken as the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to drop to 3/4 of its initial value. If the rate constant for a first order reaction is $k$, the $t_{1/4}$ can be written as
Which among the following is the most reactive ?
questions.explanation:
Interhalogen compounds are generally **more reactive** than the halogens themselves (except F₂): the X–X′ bond between two different halogens is polar and weaker than the X–X bond.
So ICl is more reactive than Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

questions.text: The structure of the major product formed in the following reaction is :
questions.explanation:
AgCN is mainly covalent (Ag–C bond), so the cyanide attacks through **nitrogen** → isocyanide (–NC). (KCN, being ionic, gives nitriles.)
Only the reactive **benzylic** –CH₂Cl is substituted; aryl halides (Ar–I, Ar–Br) don't undergo this nucleophilic substitution.
Product: the benzylic isocyanide, option (b).

questions.text: Major product formed in the following reaction is a mixture of:
questions.explanation:
HI protonates the ether oxygen. One alkyl group is **tertiary**, so the C–O bond breaks by $\mathrm{S_N1}$ to give the stable tert-butyl carbocation, which picks up I⁻ → tert-butyl iodide $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CI}$.
The other fragment leaves as cyclohexanol.
Product: cyclohexanol + $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C–I}$, option (d).

questions.text: Which of the following reagents/ reactions will convert 'A' to 'B'?

options.text: HBr, hydrolysis followed by oxidation by $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$

questions.explanation:
A has an exocyclic $\mathrm{C=CH_2}$; B has $\mathrm{–CHO}$ on that carbon (one extra carbon kept).
Hydroboration–oxidation adds water **anti-Markovnikov** → primary alcohol $\mathrm{–CH_2OH}$. PCC then oxidises a 1° alcohol only as far as the aldehyde.
Ozonolysis (b) would cut off the $\mathrm{CH_2}$ and give a ketone; the HBr route (d) gives the Markovnikov 3° product.

questions.text: Which of the following salt solutions would coagulate the colloid solution formed when $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ is added to NaOH solution, at the fastest rate?
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ added to **excess NaOH** gives $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ that adsorbs OH⁻ → a **negatively** charged sol.
It is coagulated by **cations**; by the Hardy–Schulze rule, the higher the charge, the stronger the effect. $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ (also at the highest concentration here) coagulates fastest.
(Trap: $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ added to water gives a **positive** sol, which anions would coagulate.)

questions.text: The enthalpy change for the adsorption process and micelle formation respectively are
questions.explanation:
Adsorption is **exothermic** (surface energy decreases): $\Delta H_{ads} < 0$.
Micelle formation is **endothermic**: $\Delta H_{mic} > 0$. It is driven by entropy (the hydrophobic effect), which is why micelles form only above the Krafft temperature.

questions.text: Sugar moiety in DNA and RNA molecules respectively are
questions.explanation:
DNA = **deoxy**ribonucleic acid: sugar is β-D-2-deoxyribose (no –OH at C-2).
RNA = ribonucleic acid: sugar is β-D-ribose.

questions.text: Which one of the following is **NOT** a copolymer ?
questions.explanation:
Neoprene is a **homopolymer** of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene).
Buna-S = butadiene + styrene (the same as option (d)); PHBV = 3-hydroxybutanoic acid + 3-hydroxypentanoic acid. Those are copolymers.

questions.text: Calamine and Malachite, respectively, are the ores of :
questions.explanation: Calamine: $\mathrm{ZnCO_3}$ (zinc). Malachite: $\mathrm{CuCO_3 \cdot Cu(OH)_2}$ (copper, the green ore).

questions.text: Which of the following is used as a stabilizer during the concentration of sulphide ores?
questions.explanation: In froth flotation: pine oil / fatty acids / xanthates act as **collectors** (they make the ore particles water-repellent); **cresols** and aniline act as **froth stabilisers**.

questions.text: Vulcanization of rubber is carried out by heating a mixture of :
questions.explanation: Natural rubber is cis-polyisoprene. Vulcanisation = heating it with **sulphur** (373–415 K), which forms S cross-links between chains → harder, more elastic, less sticky rubber.

questions.text: The reaction used for preparation of soap from fat is:
questions.explanation: Saponification: fat (a triglyceride ester) + NaOH → glycerol + sodium salts of fatty acids (soap). It is the **alkaline hydrolysis** of an ester.

questions.text: Which of the following electronic configuration would be associated with the highest magnetic moment ?
questions.explanation:
Spin-only $\mu = \sqrt{n(n + 2)}$ BM, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons (Hund's rule):
3d⁷ → 3, 3d⁸ → 2, 3d³ → 3, **3d⁶ → 4**.
3d⁶: $\mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.9$ BM, the highest.

questions.text: The most common oxidation state of Lanthanoid elements is +3. Which of the following is likely to deviate easily from +3 oxidation state?
questions.explanation:
Ce: $\mathrm{[Xe]\,4f^1 5d^1 6s^2}$. Losing 4 electrons gives $\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ = $\mathrm{[Xe]\,4f^0}$, a noble-gas configuration, so Ce readily shows +4.
La³⁺ (4f⁰), Gd³⁺ (4f⁷, half-filled) and Lu³⁺ (4f¹⁴, full) are already especially stable at +3.

questions.text:
The increasing order of the reactivity of the following halides for the $\mathrm{S_N1}$ reaction is
(I) $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Cl)CH_2CH_3}$  (II) $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl}$  (III) $p$-$\mathrm{H_3CO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2Cl}$
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{S_N1}$ rate follows carbocation stability:
(II) gives a 1° carbocation (least stable) < (I) gives a 2° carbocation < (III) gives a benzylic carbocation further stabilised by the +M effect of p-OCH₃ (most stable).
Order: (II) < (I) < (III).

questions.text: The difference in the reaction of phenol with bromine in chloroform and bromine in water medium is due to:
questions.explanation:
In **CHCl₃** (low polarity): phenol stays un-ionised and Br₂ is not polarised much → mono-bromination (o- and p-bromophenol).
In **water** (polar): phenol partly ionises to the highly activated phenoxide and Br₂ is polarised → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate).
The difference comes from the polarity of the solvent.

questions.text: Identify the major product in the following reaction.
questions.explanation:
$\mathrm{OH^-}$ in ethanol on a 3° alkyl halide → **elimination** (dehydrohalogenation).
Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule: the more substituted alkene is the major product → **1-methylcyclopentene** (endocyclic, trisubstituted C=C), option (c).
Methylenecyclopentane (a) is the less substituted (Hofmann) product.

questions.text: The increasing order of nitration of the following compounds is :
questions.explanation:
Nitration uses conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3/H_2SO_4}$:
(A) aniline is **protonated** to anilinium ($\mathrm{–NH_3^+}$), strongly deactivating (−I) → slowest.
(B) chlorobenzene: −I > +M → mildly deactivated.
(D) toluene: +I/hyperconjugation → activated.
(C) anisole: strong +M of –OCH₃ → most activated.
Order: A < B < D < C.

questions.text: An element X has a body centred cubic (bcc) structure with a cell edge of 200 pm. The density of the element is 5 g cm⁻³. How many number of atoms present in 300 g of the element (Given : Avogadro Constant, $N_A = 6.0 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}$)
questions.explanation:
$d = \dfrac{ZM}{a^3 N_A}$ with $Z = 2$ (bcc), $a = 2 \times 10^{-8}$ cm, $a^3 = 8 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
$M = \dfrac{d\,a^3 N_A}{Z} = \dfrac{5 \times 8 \times 10^{-24} \times 6 \times 10^{23}}{2} = 12$ g/mol.
300 g = 25 mol ⇒ $25N_A$ atoms.

questions.text: 2 moles each of ethylene glycol and glucose are dissolved in 500 g of water. The boiling point of the resulting solution is : (Given : Ebullioscopic constant of water = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Both are non-electrolytes ($i = 1$), so just add the moles: 4 mol in 0.5 kg ⇒ $m = 8$ mol/kg.
$\Delta T_b = K_b m = 0.52 \times 8 = 4.16$ K ⇒ $T_b = 373.15 + 4.16 \approx 377.3$ K.

questions.text: When the compound shown undergoes intramolecular aldol condensation, the major product formed is :
questions.explanation:
The compound is 6-oxoheptanal: $\mathrm{CH_3CO(CH_2)_4CHO}$.
The α-carbon next to the ketone (ring side) forms the enolate, which attacks the **aldehyde** carbon (more electrophilic). This closes a **5-membered ring**.
Dehydration of the β-hydroxy ketone gives the conjugated enone: **1-acetylcyclopentene**, option (a).

questions.text: The major product of the following reaction is:
questions.explanation:
Hot alkaline $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ oxidises **any** alkyl side chain that has at least one benzylic H all the way down to –COOH, cutting off the rest of the chain.
Ethylbenzene → benzoic acid (+ CO₂), option (a).

questions.text: For 1 molal aqueous solution of the following compounds, which one will show the highest freezing point?
questions.explanation:
Fewer particles → smaller $\Delta T_f$ → **higher** freezing point.
Ions per formula unit ($i$): (a) 4, (b) 3, (c) 2, (d) 1 (non-electrolyte; all Cl inside the coordination sphere).
So (d).

questions.text: The correct order in aqueous medium of basic strength in case of methyl substituted amines is :
questions.explanation:
In water, basicity depends on +I effect **and** solvation (H-bonding) of the ammonium ion **and** steric effects.
For methyl amines: $\mathrm{Me_2NH > MeNH_2 > Me_3N > NH_3}$. $\mathrm{Me_3N}$ falls behind because its cation has only one N–H for H-bonding with water.
(In the gas phase, with no solvation, the order is simply 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃.)

questions.text: Which of the following compounds is an example of hypnotic drug ?
questions.explanation:
Amytal (amobarbital) is a barbiturate: a **hypnotic/sedative** (sleep-inducing) drug.
Seldane (terfenadine) is an antihistamine, aspartame is an artificial sweetener, and prontosil is an antibacterial sulpha drug.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct structure of L-Glucose ?
questions.explanation:
D/L is decided by the –OH on the **lowest chiral carbon** (C-5) in the Fischer projection: right = D, left = L.
D-glucose (C2→C5): R, L, R, R. L-glucose is its mirror image: **L, R, L, L** — HO on the left, OH on the right, then HO, HO on the left. That is option (a).

questions.text: In a triangle ABC, BC = 7, AC = 8, AB = $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\cos A = \dfrac{2}{3}$. If $49\cos(3C) + 42 = \dfrac{m}{n}$, where $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, then $m + n$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
$\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc} = \dfrac{64 + \alpha^2 - 49}{16\alpha} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ ⇒ $3\alpha^2 - 32\alpha + 45 = 0$ ⇒ $\alpha = 9$ (or $\tfrac{5}{3}$, rejected since $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}$).
$\cos C = \dfrac{49 + 64 - 81}{2 \cdot 7 \cdot 8} = \dfrac{2}{7}$.
$\cos 3C = 4\cos^3 C - 3\cos C = \dfrac{32}{343} - \dfrac{6}{7} = -\dfrac{262}{343}$
$49\cos 3C + 42 = -\dfrac{262}{7} + 42 = \dfrac{32}{7}$ ⇒ $m + n = 39$.

questions.text: Let the equation $x(x + 2)(12 - k) = 2$ have equal roots. Then the distance of the point $\left(k, \dfrac{k}{2}\right)$ from the line $3x + 4y + 5 = 0$ is
questions.explanation:
Let $\lambda = 12 - k$: $\lambda x^2 + 2\lambda x - 2 = 0$.
Equal roots ⇒ $D = 4\lambda^2 + 8\lambda = 0$ ⇒ $\lambda = -2$ ($\lambda = 0$ isn't a quadratic) ⇒ $k = 14$.
Point $(14, 7)$: $d = \dfrac{|42 + 28 + 5|}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \dfrac{75}{5} = 15$.

questions.text: A circle C of radius 2 lies in the second quadrant and touches both the coordinate axes. Let r be the radius of a circle that has centre at the point (2, 5) and intersects the circle C at exactly two points. If the set of all possible values of r is the interval $(\alpha, \beta)$, then $3\beta - 2\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.explanation:
C touches both axes in quadrant II ⇒ centre $(-2, 2)$, radius 2.
Distance between centres: $\sqrt{(2 + 2)^2 + (5 - 2)^2} = 5$.
Two intersection points ⇔ $|r - 2| < 5 < r + 2$ ⇒ $3 < r < 7$.
$\alpha = 3,\ \beta = 7$ ⇒ $3\beta - 2\alpha = 21 - 6 = 15$.

questions.text: Let the mean and the standard deviation of the observation 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 7, $a$, $b$ be 4 and $\sqrt{2}$ respectively. Then the mean deviation about the mode of these observations is :
questions.explanation:
Mean: $\dfrac{24 + a + b}{8} = 4$ ⇒ $a + b = 8$.
Variance 2: $\sum(x - 4)^2 = 8 \times 2 = 16$. The six known values already give $4 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 9 = 16$, so $(a - 4)^2 + (b - 4)^2 = 0$ ⇒ $a = b = 4$.
Data: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7 ⇒ mode = 4.
Mean deviation about 4 $= \dfrac{2 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 3}{8} = 1$.

questions.text: The probability, of forming a 12 persons committee from 4 engineers, 2 doctors and 10 professors containing at least 3 engineers and at least 1 doctor, is:
In how many ways can a bowler take four wickets in a single 6-ball over ?
questions.explanation: Choose which 4 of the 6 balls are wickets: $\binom{6}{4} = 15$.

questions.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x} - \sqrt{1 - x}}$
questions.explanation: Rationalise: $\dfrac{x(\sqrt{1+x} + \sqrt{1-x})}{(1 + x) - (1 - x)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{1+x} + \sqrt{1-x}}{2} \to \dfrac{2}{2} = 1$.

questions.text: The domain of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9 - x^2}}$ is
questions.explanation:
Need $9 - x^2 > 0$ (strictly: it's under a root **and** in the denominator) ⇒ $-3 < x < 3$.
Trap: (a) includes $\pm 3$, where the denominator is 0.

questions.text: The amplitude of $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5} + i\left(1 - \cos\dfrac{\pi}{5}\right)$ is
questions.explanation:
Half-angle forms: $\sin\dfrac{\pi}{5} = 2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{10}$, $1 - \cos\dfrac{\pi}{5} = 2\sin^2\dfrac{\pi}{10}$.
$z = 2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{10} + i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)$, with a positive modulus ⇒ $\arg z = \dfrac{\pi}{10}$.

questions.text: If $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{4 + x} - 2}{x}$, $x \ne 0$ be continuous at $x = 0$, then $f(0) =$
questions.explanation: $f(0) = \lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sqrt{4+x} - 2}{x} \cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{4+x} + 2}{\sqrt{4+x} + 2} = \lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4+x} + 2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.text: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos^2\theta & \sin\theta\cos\theta \\ \cos\theta\sin\theta & \sin^2\theta \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} \cos^2\phi & \sin\phi\cos\phi \\ \cos\phi\sin\phi & \sin^2\phi \end{bmatrix}$, then $AB = O$, if
questions.explanation:
Each entry of $AB$ factors out $\cos(\theta - \phi)$:
$AB = \cos(\theta - \phi)\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta\cos\phi & \cos\theta\sin\phi \\ \sin\theta\cos\phi & \sin\theta\sin\phi \end{bmatrix}$
The matrix isn't identically zero, so $AB = O$ ⇔ $\cos(\theta - \phi) = 0$ ⇔ $\theta - \phi = (2n + 1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.text: If A is a square matrix of order 3, then $|\mathrm{Adj}\,A| =$
questions.explanation: $|\mathrm{adj}\,A| = |A|^{n-1}$ for an $n \times n$ matrix. With $n = 3$: $|A|^2$.

questions.text: For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$, then $14A^{-1}$ is given by :
questions.explanation:
$|A| = 6 + 1 = 7$, $\mathrm{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ (swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal).
$14A^{-1} = \dfrac{14}{7}\,\mathrm{adj}\,A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

questions.text: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sin^2 x - \cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x}\,dx =$
questions.explanation:
Split: $\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x} - \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x - \csc^2 x$.
$\int(\sec^2 x - \csc^2 x)\,dx = \tan x + \cot x + c$.

questions.text: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{e^x(1 + x)}{\cos^2(e^x x)}\,dx$ equals
questions.explanation:
Put $t = xe^x$ ⇒ $dt = e^x(1 + x)\,dx$ — exactly the numerator.

questions.text: $\displaystyle\int_{1/4}^{1/2} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x - x^2}}$ is equal to :
questions.explanation:
Complete the square: $x - x^2 = \left(\tfrac12\right)^2 - \left(x - \tfrac12\right)^2$.
$\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{(1/2)^2 - (x - 1/2)^2}} = \sin^{-1}(2x - 1)$.
$\left[\sin^{-1}(2x - 1)\right]_{1/4}^{1/2} = \sin^{-1}0 - \sin^{-1}\left(-\tfrac12\right) = 0 + \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

questions.text: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{x + \frac{\pi}{4}}{2 - \cos 2x}\,dx$ is :
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{x}{2 - \cos 2x}$ is odd, so its integral over $[-\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{\pi}{4}]$ is 0:
$I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\dfrac{dx}{2 - \cos 2x} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{\pi/4}\dfrac{dx}{2 - \cos 2x}$
With $t = \tan x$: $2 - \cos 2x = \dfrac{1 + 3t^2}{1 + t^2}$, $dx = \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^2}$
$I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{dt}{1 + 3t^2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\sqrt3 = \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt3} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi^2}{6\sqrt3}$.

questions.text: If two straight lines whose direction cosines are given by the relations $l + m - n = 0$, $3l^2 + m^2 + cnl = 0$ are parallel, then the positive value of c is:
questions.explanation:
Substitute $n = l + m$: $3l^2 + m^2 + cl(l + m) = 0$ ⇒ $(3 + c)\left(\dfrac{l}{m}\right)^2 + c\left(\dfrac{l}{m}\right) + 1 = 0$.
The two lines are parallel ⇔ this quadratic has equal roots: $c^2 - 4(3 + c) = 0$ ⇒ $c^2 - 4c - 12 = 0$ ⇒ $c = 6$ or $-2$.
Positive value: $c = 6$.

questions.text: If the two lines $l_1: \dfrac{x - 2}{3} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-2}$, $z = 2$ and $l_2: \dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{2y + 3}{\alpha} = \dfrac{z + 5}{2}$ are perpendicular, then an angle between the lines $l_2$ and $l_3: \dfrac{1 - x}{3} = \dfrac{2y - 1}{-4} = \dfrac{z}{4}$ is :
questions.explanation:
Direction ratios (write each line in standard form first):
$l_1$: $(3, -2, 0)$; $l_2$: $(1, \tfrac{\alpha}{2}, 2)$; $l_3$: $\dfrac{x - 1}{-3} = \dfrac{y - \frac12}{-2} = \dfrac{z}{4}$ ⇒ $(-3, -2, 4)$.
$l_1 \perp l_2$: $3 - \alpha = 0$ ⇒ $\alpha = 3$, so $l_2$: $(1, \tfrac32, 2)$.
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{|-3 - 3 + 8|}{\sqrt{1 + \frac94 + 4}\,\sqrt{9 + 4 + 16}} = \dfrac{2}{\frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}\sqrt{29}} = \dfrac{4}{29}$
$\theta = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{4}{29} = \sec^{-1}\dfrac{29}{4}$. (Option (a) is impossible: cosine can't exceed 1.)

questions.text: If the plane $x - 3y + 5z = d$ passes through the point (1, 2, 4), then the length of intercepts cut by it on the axes of X, Y, Z are respectively, is
questions.explanation: $d = 1 - 6 + 20 = 15$. Intercept form: $\dfrac{x}{15} + \dfrac{y}{-5} + \dfrac{z}{3} = 1$ ⇒ intercepts 15, −5, 3.

questions.text: The maximum value of $P = x + 3y$ such that $2x + y \le 20$, $x + 2y \le 20$, $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$ is
questions.explanation:
Corner points of the feasible region and $P = x + 3y$:
$(0, 0)$: 0; $(10, 0)$: 10; $(0, 10)$: **30**; $\left(\tfrac{20}{3}, \tfrac{20}{3}\right)$: $\tfrac{80}{3} \approx 26.7$.
Maximum $P = 30$ at $(0, 10)$.
Note: the published key for this paper marks (d) "None", even though its own working finds $P = 30$ at $(0, 10)$. The correct answer is (c).

questions.text: Corner points of feasible region of inequalities gives
questions.explanation: Corner point theorem: if an LPP has an optimal solution, it occurs at a **corner (vertex) of the feasible region**. Evaluating the objective at the corner points gives the optimal solution.

questions.text: If $P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}$, $P(B) = 0$, then $P(A/B)$ is
questions.explanation: $P(A|B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$ requires $P(B) \ne 0$. Here $P(B) = 0$, so it is **not defined**.

questions.text: Under what condition do $\left\langle \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \dfrac{1}{2}, k \right\rangle$ represent direction cosines of a line?
questions.explanation: Direction cosines satisfy $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$: $\dfrac12 + \dfrac14 + k^2 = 1$ ⇒ $k^2 = \dfrac14$ ⇒ $k = \pm\dfrac12$.

questions.text: The lines $x = ay + b$, $z = cy + d$ and $x = a'y + b'$, $z = c'y + d'$ are perpendicular if
questions.explanation:
Symmetric form of the first line: $\dfrac{x - b}{a} = \dfrac{y}{1} = \dfrac{z - d}{c}$ ⇒ direction ratios $(a, 1, c)$. Second line: $(a', 1, c')$.
Perpendicular ⇔ $aa' + 1 \cdot 1 + cc' = 0$.

questions.text: Let X be a binomially distributed random variable with mean 4 and variance $\dfrac{4}{3}$. Then $54\,P(X \le 2)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
$np = 4$, $npq = \tfrac43$ ⇒ $q = \tfrac13$, $p = \tfrac23$, $n = 6$.
$P(X \le 2) = \dfrac{\binom60 + \binom61 \cdot 2 + \binom62 \cdot 4}{3^6} = \dfrac{1 + 12 + 60}{729} = \dfrac{73}{729}$
$54 \times \dfrac{73}{729} = \dfrac{146}{27}$.

questions.text: The mean and variance of a random variable X having binomial distribution are 4 and 2 respectively, then $P(X = 1)$ is
questions.explanation:
$q = \dfrac{npq}{np} = \dfrac12$ ⇒ $p = \dfrac12$, $n = 8$.
$P(X = 1) = \binom81\left(\dfrac12\right)^8 = \dfrac{8}{256} = \dfrac{1}{32}$.

questions.text: Four fair dice are thrown independently 27 times. Then the expected number of times, at least two dice show up a three or a five, is
questions.explanation:
Per die, $P(3 \text{ or } 5) = \dfrac13$. For one throw of 4 dice:
$P(\text{at least 2}) = 1 - \left(\dfrac23\right)^4 - \binom41\dfrac13\left(\dfrac23\right)^3 = 1 - \dfrac{16}{81} - \dfrac{32}{81} = \dfrac{33}{81} = \dfrac{11}{27}$
Expected count over 27 throws: $27 \times \dfrac{11}{27} = 11$.

questions.text: The area bounded by the curve $y = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}$, the line $x = 1$ and $x$-axis is ______ sq. units.
questions.explanation: $A = \displaystyle\int_0^1 \dfrac32\sqrt{x}\,dx = \dfrac32 \cdot \dfrac23\left[x^{3/2}\right]_0^1 = 1$ sq. unit.

questions.text: The area bounded by $y - 1 = |x|$, $y = 0$ and $|x| = \dfrac{1}{2}$ will be:
questions.explanation:
$y = 1 + |x|$ is symmetric about the y-axis:
$A = 2\displaystyle\int_0^{1/2}(1 + x)\,dx = 2\left[x + \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^{1/2} = 2\left(\dfrac12 + \dfrac18\right) = \dfrac54$.

questions.text: $\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}y = c$ is the general solution of the differential equation
questions.explanation:
Differentiate: $\dfrac{dx}{1 + x^2} + \dfrac{dy}{1 + y^2} = 0$ ⇒ multiply by $(1 + x^2)(1 + y^2)$: $(1 + y^2)\,dx + (1 + x^2)\,dy = 0$.
(a) is missing the minus sign: the correct slope is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1 + y^2}{1 + x^2}$.

If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$ are three non-coplanar vectors, then $[\vec{a} + \vec{b} + \vec{c}\ \ \vec{a} - \vec{c}\ \ \vec{a} - \vec{b}]$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
$(\vec a - \vec c) \times (\vec a - \vec b) = -\vec a \times \vec b - \vec c \times \vec a - \vec b \times \vec c$ (using $\vec a \times \vec a = 0$, $\vec c \times \vec b = -\vec b \times \vec c$)
Dot with $\vec a + \vec b + \vec c$: only the terms containing all three vectors survive, each $= -[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$:
$-[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c] - [\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c] - [\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c] = -3[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$.
Shortcut: the coefficient determinant $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\1&0&-1\\1&-1&0\end{vmatrix} = -3$.

questions.text: The vectors $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + m\hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + (m + 1)\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + m\hat{k}$ are coplanar if m is equal to
questions.explanation:
Coplanar ⇔ $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & m \\ 1 & 1 & m+1 \\ 1 & -1 & m \end{vmatrix} = 0$.
Subtract row 1 from rows 2 and 3: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & m \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 1(0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot (-2)) = 2$.
It equals 2 for **every** m, never 0, so no value of m works: None.

questions.text: If A, B and C are the vertices of a triangle whose position vectors are $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ respectively and G is the centroid of the $\triangle ABC$, then $\overrightarrow{GA} + \overrightarrow{GB} + \overrightarrow{GC}$ is
questions.explanation:
$\vec g = \dfrac{\vec a + \vec b + \vec c}{3}$.
$\overrightarrow{GA} + \overrightarrow{GB} + \overrightarrow{GC} = (\vec a + \vec b + \vec c) - 3\vec g = \vec 0$.

questions.text: If $x = b\cos^{-1}\sqrt{\dfrac{y}{b}} + \sqrt{by - y^2}$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} =$
questions.explanation:
Differentiate w.r.t. $y$:
$\dfrac{d}{dy}\left[b\cos^{-1}\sqrt{\tfrac{y}{b}}\right] = -\dfrac{b}{\sqrt{1 - y/b}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{by}} = -\dfrac{b}{2\sqrt{by - y^2}}$
$\dfrac{d}{dy}\sqrt{by - y^2} = \dfrac{b - 2y}{2\sqrt{by - y^2}}$
$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{-b + b - 2y}{2\sqrt{by - y^2}} = -\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{by - y^2}}$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{by - y^2}}{y} = -\sqrt{\dfrac{b}{y} - 1}$.
Note: the published key lists (b), but its own working arrives at $-\sqrt{b/y - 1}$, which is option (a).

questions.text: If $y = e^{x^x}$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} =$
questions.explanation:
Chain rule: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x^x} \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^x)$, and $\dfrac{d}{dx}x^x = x^x(1 + \ln x)$ (log-differentiate $x^x$).
So $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\,x^x(1 + \log_e x)$, option (b).
Note: the answer-key table in this paper prints (d), but its worked solution gives (b).

questions.text: If $f(1) = 1$, $f'(1) = 3$, then the derivative of $f(f(f(x))) + (f(x))^2$ at $x = 1$ is :
questions.explanation:
$g'(x) = f'(f(f(x))) \cdot f'(f(x)) \cdot f'(x) + 2f(x)f'(x)$.
At $x = 1$ every inner value is $f(1) = 1$: $g'(1) = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 3 = 27 + 6 = 33$.

questions.text: Which of the following functions is differentiable at $x = 0$?
questions.explanation:
$\cos|x| = \cos x$ is smooth, so (a), (b) inherit the corner of $|x|$ → not differentiable.
Near 0, $\sin|x| \approx |x|$:
(c) $\sin|x| + |x| \approx 2|x|$: LHD −2, RHD 2 → corner.
(d) $\sin|x| - |x|$: LHD $= \lim \dfrac{\sin h - h}{-h} = 0$, RHD $= \lim \dfrac{\sin h - h}{h} = 0$ → differentiable. The corners cancel.

questions.text: Let $f(x) = |\sin x|$. Then

options.text: f is everywhere continuous but not differentiable at $x = n\pi$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$
f is everywhere continuous but not differentiable at $x = (2n + 1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$

questions.explanation:
$|\sin x|$ is continuous (composition of continuous functions). It has sharp corners where $\sin x$ crosses zero, i.e. at $x = n\pi$ (slope jumps from −1 to +1).
At $x = (2n + 1)\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ the graph has smooth peaks, so it **is** differentiable there.

questions.text: The approximate values of $\sqrt{0.0037}$ is
questions.explanation:
Take $x = 0.0036$ ($\sqrt{x} = 0.06$), $\Delta x = 0.0001$.
$\sqrt{x + \Delta x} \approx \sqrt{x} + \dfrac{\Delta x}{2\sqrt x} = 0.06 + \dfrac{0.0001}{0.12} = 0.06 + \dfrac{1}{1200} = \dfrac{73}{1200}$.

questions.text: If $f(x) = x^x$, then $f(x)$ is decreasing in interval :
questions.explanation:
$f'(x) = x^x(1 + \ln x)$. Since $x^x > 0$, $f' < 0$ ⇔ $\ln x < -1$ ⇔ $x < \dfrac1e$.
So $f$ is decreasing on $\left]0, \tfrac1e\right[$.

questions.text: If $x = a(\cos t + t\sin t)$ and $y = a(\sin t - t\cos t)$, then $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is
questions.explanation:
$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a(-\sin t + \sin t + t\cos t) = at\cos t$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = a(\cos t - \cos t + t\sin t) = at\sin t$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \tan t$
$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(\tan t) \cdot \dfrac{dt}{dx} = \dfrac{\sec^2 t}{at\cos t} = \dfrac{\sec^3 t}{at}$.

questions.text: The maximum value of $(\log x)/x$ is
questions.explanation:
$y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}$ ⇒ $y' = \dfrac{1 - \ln x}{x^2} = 0$ ⇒ $x = e$ (y′ changes from + to −, so this is a maximum).
Maximum value $= \dfrac{\ln e}{e} = \dfrac1e$.
Trap: $e$ is where the maximum occurs, not its value.

questions.text: $\sim((\sim p) \wedge q)$ is equal to
questions.explanation:
De Morgan: $\sim(A \wedge B) = \sim A \vee \sim B$.
$\sim((\sim p) \wedge q) = \sim(\sim p) \vee \sim q = p \vee (\sim q)$.

questions.text: Let p: price increases, q: Demand falls. The symbolic statement of 'If demand does not fall then price does not increase' is
questions.explanation: "Demand does not fall" = $\sim q$ (hypothesis); "price does not increase" = $\sim p$ (conclusion). "If … then …" is $\to$: $\sim q \to \sim p$.

questions.text: The angle between two lines represented by $2x^2 + 5xy + 3y^2 + 6x + 7y + 4 = 0$ is
questions.explanation:
For $ax^2 + 2hxy + by^2 + \ldots = 0$: $\tan\theta = \pm\dfrac{2\sqrt{h^2 - ab}}{a + b}$ (only the second-degree terms matter).
$a = 2,\ h = \tfrac52,\ b = 3$: $\tan\theta = \pm\dfrac{2\sqrt{\frac{25}{4} - 6}}{5} = \pm\dfrac{2 \cdot \frac12}{5} = \pm\dfrac15$.

questions.text: If one of the lines of $6x^2 - xy + 4cy^2 = 0$ is given by $3x + 4y = 0$, then c equals
questions.explanation:
Every point of $3x + 4y = 0$, i.e. $y = -\tfrac34x$, must satisfy the pair:
$6x^2 + \dfrac34x^2 + 4c \cdot \dfrac{9}{16}x^2 = 0$ ⇒ $6 + \dfrac34 + \dfrac{9c}{4} = 0$ ⇒ $c = -3$.

questions.text: If $y = mx + 4$ is a tangent to both the parabolas, $y^2 = 4x$ and $x^2 = 2by$, then b is equal to:
questions.explanation:
Tangent to $y^2 = 4ax$ ($a = 1$): $c = \dfrac{a}{m}$ ⇒ $4 = \dfrac1m$ ⇒ $m = \dfrac14$.
Substitute $y = \tfrac{x}{4} + 4$ into $x^2 = 2by$: $x^2 = 2b\left(\dfrac{x + 16}{4}\right)$ ⇒ $2x^2 - bx - 16b = 0$.
Tangent ⇒ $D = 0$: $b^2 + 128b = 0$ ⇒ $b = -128$ ($b = 0$ isn't a parabola).

questions.text: The tangents to the hyperbola $x^2 - y^2 = 3$ are parallel to the st line $2x + y + 8 = 0$ at the following points
questions.explanation:
Slope needed: −2. Differentiating, $2x - 2yy' = 0$ ⇒ $y' = \dfrac{x}{y} = -2$ ⇒ $x = -2y$.
On the curve: $4y^2 - y^2 = 3$ ⇒ $y = \pm1$, $x = \mp2$ ⇒ points $(2, -1)$ and $(-2, 1)$.
Check: $4 - 1 = 3$ ✓.
